templates.system: Write a short between-innings radio ad in the deadpan-absurd register of Tim Robinson, I Think You Should Leave, and SNL fake commercials. [S1] and [S2] are two people having a private conversation — they are NOT addressing the audience. [S1] is asking probing, casual questions about [S2]'s use of the product. [S2] gives answers that are too specific, too matter-of-fact, or that reveal a small concerning detail of their life without ever acknowledging it as strange. The humor is entirely in the subtext — what [S2] is implying without saying, what [S1] keeps almost calling out but doesn't. Both characters take the product completely seriously. RULES: No alliteration. No wordplay or puns. No exclamation points. No 'wherever fine X are sold' or 'ask your grocer' tagline cliches. No rhyming. Use ONE concrete proper noun (a person's name, a place, a brand-adjacent specific) that grounds the scene. 8-12 short lines total. Each line is one or two sentences max — natural speech, not announcer voice. Format every line with [S1] or [S2] tag. Alternate speakers. The last spoken line should be a product tag delivered like an afterthought, with a weird qualifier or strange phrasing. ALWAYS end with the OPPOSITE empty tag (e.g., last spoken line '[S1]...' → final tag '[S2]'). Never spell out units.

Write a short between-innings radio ad in the deadpan-absurd register of Tim Robinson, I Think You Should Leave, and SNL fake commercials. [S1] is a salesperson at a trade show or demonstration booth pitching the product with unwavering enthusiasm. [S2] is a customer who keeps asking clarifying questions that surface disturbing or absurd implications of the product. [S1] never breaks pitch character — every concerning implication [S2] surfaces, [S1] reframes as a selling point. The humor comes from [S1]'s unshakeable enthusiasm in the face of [S2]'s growing unease, which is never named. RULES: No alliteration. No wordplay or puns. No rhyming. [S1] never acknowledges anything is wrong. Use ONE concrete physical detail about the product (a sound it makes, what it feels like in the hand, what it leaves behind, a smell). 8-12 short lines total. Natural speech, not announcer voice — even [S1] is a person, not a 1940s radio voice. Format every line with [S1] or [S2] tag. Alternate speakers. ALWAYS end with the OPPOSITE empty tag. Never spell out units.

Write a short between-innings radio ad in the deadpan-absurd register of Tim Robinson, I Think You Should Leave, and SNL fake commercials. [S2] is a satisfied customer speaking sincerely about how the product has changed their life. As they talk, their enthusiasm reveals progressively weirder or sadder details about their life — delivered matter-of-factly, never framed as a punchline. The customer would not say any of this is strange. [S1] is an announcer who appears only at the very end, exactly one line, delivered flat — a product tag with a slightly off qualifier. RULES: No alliteration. No wordplay or puns. No exclamation points. No rhyming. Use ONE concrete proper noun (a name, a town, a workplace) that grounds the scene. 8-12 short lines total. [S2] does ~85% of the talking. [S1] enters only on the final spoken line. Format every line with [S1] or [S2] tag. ALWAYS end with the OPPOSITE empty tag (so if the announcer's [S1] line is last, finish with empty [S2]). Never spell out units.
